title: The sign
hookLine: close your eyes and the image stays. then the manual says the real one has no color and no shape.
tomorrow: why would anyone meditate on a skeleton?

cards: Stare at a bright window for a while, then close your eyes, and a glowing rectangle floats there in odd colors before it fades. That's the eye, worn out.
Buddhaghosa describes something that sounds similar and isn't, and it answers yesterday's question: why does the image stay after you close your eyes? He calls it the sign, nimitta.
Then he says something strange about it. The sign that matters most, the steady one, has no color and no shape. How can the image of a round disc have no shape?

teach.h: FIRST, THE DISC YOU LOOK AT.
teach.b: Take it in stages. First there's the disc itself: clay, water, blue flowers, the thing you look at. Look, close your eyes, look again.

When the disc appears as clearly with your eyes closed as open, the manual says, the learned sign has arisen. That's why the image stays: you've taken it in so thoroughly that the mind can hold it without the eyes.
It still carries the disc's flaws, a thumbprint in the clay, a stray stalk. Keep going, and the counterpart sign can arise, breaking out of the first one, far purer.
His similes: a mirror taken from its case, a mother-of-pearl dish washed clean, the moon coming out from behind a cloud. And here the puzzle solves itself.

teach.h: THEN PURER: NO COLOR, NO SHAPE.
teach.b: It has no color and no shape, he says, because it isn't something the eye sees. It's born of perception, in a mind that has gathered. It's less a picture of the disc than a sign that the mind has settled.
That's why he treats it as precious.

teach.h: GUARD IT, LIKE A CARRIED CHILD.
teach.b: Guard it, he says, the way a queen guards the child she's carrying.
Not to show it off. So it can grow.

how: In Theravada meditation teaching, the learning sign and the counterpart sign mark stages of concentration on a kasina, as Visuddhimagga 4 describes; students usually report them to a teacher rather than judging them alone.

o: the inner image that forms when an object is well learned
an omen from the gods that shows what will happen next
a hand gesture monks make with their fingers while chanting

games.q: the stages of the sign — tap the pairs.
p: as clear with eyes closed as open
like a queen guards her unborn child

s: the counterpart sign is just a sharper picture of the disc
Buddhaghosa says it has no color or shape; it's born of perception in a settled mind.
the learned sign arises when the disc appears as clearly with eyes closed as open
that's why the image stays: the mind has taken it in.
the glowing shape after staring at a light is the nimitta
that's tired eyes. the learned sign is the object taken in so well it appears clearly with eyes closed.

games.q: a classmate says she saw a bright light while meditating, so she must be nearly enlightened. what's a careful reply, by today's lesson?
o: a sign marks a settling mind, not the end of the path. guard it, don't hype it.
she's practically there; a bright light is the sign the old texts promise.
lights mean something has gone wrong, so she should stop meditating.
games.why: Buddhaghosa treats the sign as a stage of concentration, to be guarded like a carried child, not as proof of awakening.

practice: Look at one simple object near you for a few breaths: a cup, a round coaster, a spot of light. Then close your eyes and notice what of it stays, without forcing anything.
When it fades, open your eyes, look again, and close them again.

wordCard.voice: Nimitta: the sign. The inner image of the object, first learned, then purer, with no color or shape at all.

orig.note: Pali: sign, mark, image. In meditation manuals, the inner image of the object: learned, then counterpart.

carryVoice: Your line: the sign appears, and then it's guarded, like something precious. Day sixteen of forty.

sources.ref: Visuddhimagga 4 (the earth kasina: the learning sign arises when the kasina appears as clearly with eyes shut as open, still showing the kasina's faults; the counterpart sign breaks out of it, far more purified, like a mirror taken from its case, a well-washed mother-of-pearl dish, the moon's disc coming out from behind a cloud; it has neither color nor shape and is born of perception; it is to be guarded like the embryo of a wheel-turning monarch)
